wa_warrior_peak_standard.name: Upper Dungeness Trail, Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter to the southeast cirque
wa_warrior_peak_standard.notes:
From US-101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn on Louella Road for a mile, then Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles, becoming FS Road 28 at the forest boundary. Right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required at the kiosk.

Trail #833.2 is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike 3.2-3.4 miles and about 600 ft to Camp Handy at roughly 3,100 ft, a riverfront meadow with a cedar-shingle shelter, then take the uphill fork and continue about 3 miles and 1,850 ft to Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at 6.3-6.4 miles and roughly 4,890-4,950 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the approach.

From Boulder Shelter hike south on the Dungeness / Constance Pass trail, crossing several creeks, toward Home Lake.
wa_warrior_peak_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the summit couloir into early season is an improvement on the scree that replaces it
hazards: Loose, poor-quality rock on the final headwall above the 7,000 ft saddle — a recurring theme in every account
Rockfall in the couloir between the twin summits, worst with parties above or after freeze-thaw
Glissade and uncontrolled-slide risk descending the snow chute if the runout is not fully visible — one party described nearly going over a cliff band on nearby terrain
Faint use-trail-only route-finding above the trail through forest, meadow and talus
Fast-moving Pacific frontal systems and late-summer afternoon thunderstorms
wa_warrior_peak_standard.baseFinding:
The first test is a creek you must not cross. Leave the trail before crossing the major stream that drains the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque. That stream is the last and largest of the several you meet going south from Boulder Shelter. Then climb east — steep forest, then steep open meadow, then talus — staying north of the streambed the whole way. The streambed is the handrail and it stays on your right. If you have crossed it and it is now on your left, you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

The arrival test is the cirque at about 5,900 ft, and it is unambiguous because it is a closed basin: the ground stops rising in front of you and the headwall closes round. From there, head north to the obvious couloir between the two peaks. Warrior has twin summits and the couloir runs up between them to a saddle at about 7,000 ft. There is one gully in that headwall with a summit on each side of it. If the gully you are in has a summit on only one side, it is not the one.

The test at the top of the couloir is which way to turn, and it is the single most useful sentence for this peak in fog: at the saddle, the higher peak is on your right. The southeast summit is the true top; the northwest summit at roughly 7,285 ft is the lower one. Coming up the couloir from the cirque, the true summit is to the right. Turn left and you will climb the wrong peak on ground just as loose.

Second test, on the summit block: above the saddle there is 20 to 50 feet of exposed, poor-quality rock rated Class 4 to low fifth on the block's northwest side, often gained over steep snow or a snow moat, and many parties fix a hand line on it. If your last obstacle before the top is a walk rather than a short difficult rock step, you are on the wrong summit.

What the season changes: the couloir is steep but straightforward when snow-filled, common early season; melted out it is a brutal scree slog to the same saddle. Both are the route.

wa_warrior_peak_standard.name: Home Lake basecamp, from either the Dungeness or the Dosewallips side
wa_warrior_peak_standard.notes:
Home Lake at about 5,308-5,330 ft, walled in by Mount Constance and Warrior Peak just below Constance Pass, is the standard basecamp for this climb and it is reachable from two directions: north up the Upper Dungeness / Constance Pass trail at roughly 9.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, or south from the Dosewallips road end over Constance Pass. An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required.

Camping at Home Lake rather than pushing from Boulder Shelter turns this into a comfortable two-day trip and puts you a mile from the cirque. It is also the camp shared with Mount Fricaba, Mount Mystery and Mount Deception parties, so it is well-used ground with an established site.

From the lake, leave the basin and climb east into the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque through meadow and talus.
hazards: Same as the Boulder Shelter variant: loose summit rock, couloir rockfall, glissade runout, faint route-finding
Home Lake sits below Constance Pass, so an exit north regains meaningful height before the long descent
Wilderness permit required and the site is popular with parties climbing four different peaks
wa_warrior_peak_standard.baseFinding: From Home Lake the test is the same streambed, worked from the other end: walk back north along the trail to the stream that drains the cirque, the last and largest creek the trail crosses before the lake, and climb east beside it, staying north of the streambed. The stream is the handrail either way, and once you are climbing it stays on your right. The arrival test is the same closed cirque at about 5,900 ft, and then the obvious couloir between the two peaks running north to the saddle at about 7,000 ft — the one gully with a summit on each side of it. And the same turn at the top: at the saddle the higher, true summit is on your right (southeast). The 20 to 50 ft Class 4 / low fifth step on the block's northwest side is the last obstacle; if there is no step, you are on the northwest summit. Honest limit: this variant differs from the one above only in where you sleep and which direction you walk in. It is recorded separately because the route is titled for the Home Lake approach and a reader should not have to reconcile that with an approach description that starts from Boulder Shelter.

wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.name: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.notes:
Park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass at about 4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff. Leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs. There is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT.

This is Whistler Mountain above Rainy Pass in Chelan County, not the Whistler Canyon trailhead area near Oroville, which is about 100 miles away and unrelated.

Round trip runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain.
hazards: No maintained tread above the PCT; steep cross-country through timber and over downed logs
Rock gully with downsloping slabs and loose gravel near the summit, rockfall from parties above
Loose talus and scree in the gullies with class 3-4 moves and exposure near the crest
Lingering snow in forest and basin firms or ices the gullies early season
Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies in spring snow season
No reliable water above the lower forest
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.baseFinding:
Climb until the forest opens. At about 6,100 ft the timber gives way to A meadow basin below the west ridge and gully complex, and that transition is the first reliable confirmation on a trail-less approach. Trees stopping is something you notice in any visibility.

From the basin, trend south and southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col and basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat. That col is the aiming point, and it is named by the two peaks either side of it.

Then work up the broad west ridge, or the shallow gully just north of it, to the summit shoulder.

The last section is the one that confirms you are on the summit line rather than a neighbouring gully: a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall, over downsloping slabs and loose gravel. A ramp cutting the headwall is the way through; helmet on here for rockfall from parties above.

wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.name: The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft

approachLogistics.trailhead: Unmarked SR-20 pullout about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass

wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.notes:
The second option, and the one that reaches the true south ridge. From the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass, 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, at about 5,000 ft, walk back down and along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees.

About 4 miles round trip with roughly 3,000 ft of gain, the same as the PCT option.
hazards: Unmarked pullout on SR-20 found only by distance from the Blue Lake trailhead; walk along the road shoulder
Trail-less above the first stretch of forest
Class 2-3 with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest
Loose talus and scree in the connecting gullies
Wet-slab and cornice avalanche danger in the gullies in spring snow season
No reliable water on the route
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
wa_whistler_mountain_scramble.baseFinding:
The trailhead is unmarked and the path start is a tree-line edge, so the find is at the road rather than on the mountain. The pullout is 0.7 mile before the Blue Lake Trailhead coming from Rainy Pass. If you have reached the Blue Lake Trailhead, you have driven 0.7 mile too far. From the pullout, walk the shoulder to where a stand of trees begins, and the boot path leaves from its west edge.

Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. A level section of ridge is the arrival, and a level stretch on a ridge is something you can feel underfoot without seeing anything.

From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit. The alternative, which is also correct: leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left, west, onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish that way.

So the decision at 6,800 ft is a real fork and both branches work: stay on the crest for more exposure and directness, or cross two gullies west for easier ground.

The negative test against the other approach, which matters because both start within three miles of each other on the same highway: the PCT option leaves from the marked PCT North lot at Rainy Pass and gains a meadow basin at 6,100 ft below the west ridge. This one leaves from an unmarked turnout and gains the south ridge at 6,180 ft. Marked lot and west ridge, or unmarked turnout and south ridge.

wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.name: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.notes:
Niederprum trailhead at the end of Old Mine Road above Darrington. The Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded for years, so parties park at the gate, get past the barricade on foot and walk the road roughly a mile and a quarter to the real trailhead — extra distance and gain that older published figures do not include.

Trail #653 switchbacks through forest into the Boulder River Wilderness and reaches 'the flat' at about 3,200 ft, a level clearing on the site of an old mining cabin and the natural rest or camp spot. Beyond it the maintained tread ends and a boot path threads thinning, brushy forest with deadfall.

Above that the route traverses south through moderately dense forest between roughly 4,500 and 4,700 ft to reach a broad snow couloir, which is climbed to Lone Tree Pass at about 5,000 ft. From the pass, traverse east along the ridge and then drop several hundred feet southeast to a small lake and flat meadow — a sheltered bivy. A long rising traverse east below cliff bands then leads to a broad gully up to High Pass at about 6,100 ft, and over it onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier.
wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.season: late Apr-Jun for snow cover; the line goes later but on more rock
hazards: barricaded Moose Creek bridge at the start
avalanche terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass
vague, brushy route-finding with deadfall above 'the flat'
crevasses on the Whitehorse Glacier from roughly July onward
summit bergschrund and moat, often a fifth-class or roped step by midsummer
no reliable water once you are on snow
wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.baseFinding:
Lone Tree Pass cannot be picked out from directly beneath it, and that is the single most useful thing to know about this approach. Look at the mountain from the valley before you start — from the highway at Darrington — and fix where the pass sits relative to the shoulder, because once you are traversing inside the forest between 4,500 and 4,700 ft there is nothing to aim at. The confirmation from inside the trees is the ground itself: you are traversing, not climbing, and the correct entry is where that traversing forest opens into a broad snow couloir. A narrow gully or a steep timbered rib is not it.

For the upper half, the landmark is White Benchmark, Point 6357 — a blocky tower that works as a lighthouse for the whole rising traverse to High Pass. Keep it in view and aim at it; the broad gully up to the pass is right there. If you have run out of the rising traverse without a blocky tower above you, you are low and short of the pass.

The climbing itself starts at High Pass, where you cross onto the glacier. Snow travel of up to about thirty-five degrees leads to the summit snow ridge. The final marker is at the very top: by midsummer the bergschrund and moat below the summit rock often force a short section of fifth-class rock or a delicate roped step across a snow bridge, so the route does not simply walk out on snow.

wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.name: Snow Gulch direct (deep snow only)
wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.notes: A more direct line used by some early-season and ski parties. From the Niederprum trailhead area, follow the old forest-road grade toward Snow Gulch, then ascend the creek drainage. The section between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft is a steep bushwhack through slide alder or up the adjacent slabs, and it only makes sense once deep snow has buried the brush. Parties commonly stash skis or boards around 2,500 ft in the old growth for the descent.
wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.season: early season, deep snow burying the brush
hazards: slide alder and slabs between roughly 1,100 and 2,200 ft when snow cover is thin
avalanche hazard in the gulch and on the glacier headwall in the early-season window
wa_whitehorse_mountain_nw_shoulder.baseFinding: This variation rejoins the same upper ground, so the markers are unchanged: White Benchmark (Point 6357) for the traverse to High Pass, and High Pass itself as the step onto the glacier. The specific trap here is timing rather than terrain — if you are fighting slide alder rather than walking on snow, the line is out of condition and the standard Niederprum trail is the better choice that day.

wa_wild_wild_west.name: Road walk from the pullout to the foot of the wall
wa_wild_wild_west.notes: From Randle, head south and follow the main forest road roughly nineteen miles, then turn off at the signed meadows turning and follow the next road under three miles before turning again onto the last one. That final road is rough and wants high clearance; follow it about two miles until the rock appears, then carry on to the large pullout where the climbers' trail is obvious. From the pullout, simply walk up the road toward the wall and onto its base. There is no cell service on the approach or at the crag.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia studded with cobbles and knobs that can pop loose without warning
Rough gravel approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service on the approach or at the crag
The formation's base wraps a long way; the toe is a specific point, not a general area
wa_wild_wild_west.baseFinding: Go to the lowest toe of the West Face — the point where the wall's base comes down closest to the road, rather than anywhere along its higher flanks. The start is a short prow, and the test is bolts you can count: two of them, low, on the prow, within reach from the ground. Confirm from the pitches above — the first climbs a short face onto clean ramps to a ledge belay, and the second traverses across a saddle to a chain anchor, which is a distinctive shape for a second pitch and not something a neighbouring line does. Negative marker: if you are under a long face with no bolts within reach of the ground and the only protection on offer is slinging the embedded cobbles and knobs, you are on one of the older knob-slinging lines rather than this bolted one.

wa_wild_wild_west.name: Around the East Face and through the Gap
wa_wild_wild_west.notes: The other way onto this side of the formation, and the one to use if you are coming from routes on the far side. From the same pullout, take the climbers' trail around the east face of the rock — this trail traverses the whole formation — and pass through the deep gully that splits it, then drop down to the left onto the West Face's base. It is longer than walking up the road but it links the two sides without returning to the car.
hazards: Volcanic tuff-breccia with loose cobbles and knobs
The traverse round the formation is on climbers' trail with loose ground below the walls
Rough approach roads needing high clearance
No cell service anywhere on the approach or at the crag
wa_wild_wild_west.baseFinding: Having dropped down and left out of the walk-through gully, keep descending along the base until you reach the lowest toe of the West Face — the far low point of the wall, not the first rock you meet after the gap. The start is a short prow carrying two bolts within reach of the ground. Confirm above: a short face to clean ramps and a ledge belay, then a traverse across a saddle to a chain anchor. Negative markers: if the deep walk-through gully is still behind and above you and you have not dropped down and left, you are on the flank rather than at the foot of the face; if you are looking at a long unbolted face where knobs are the only protection, you are on an older line.

wa_windy_peak_trail.name: Trail 342 from Long Swamp
wa_windy_peak_trail.notes: This is the easternmost of the high peaks here and by far the least technical, being a trail walk with a very short scramble stapled on the end, so the real work is the drive. Long gravel forest roads out of Loomis reach Long Swamp Campground, where Trail 342 starts and climbs steadily through burned lodgepole and recovering meadow to a camp with water partway up and then out onto open, treeless ridge. A shorter trail comes in from the Cathedral Driveway trailhead a few miles further west but is overgrown in stretches from lack of use, and a third start at Iron Gate involves the roughest driving of the three. Water on the upper trail is limited and seasonal, so carry enough for a long day.
hazards: Long trail mileage with limited seasonal water on the upper half
Fully exposed, treeless ridge and summit in wind and lightning
Faint braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch to the true summit
Standing fire-killed snags along the burned lower trail in wind
Long gravel forest road driving far from any town, no cell coverage
wa_windy_peak_trail.baseFinding: The trail does not go to the top, which is the single most useful thing to know here. Tread climbs to a junction and high point below and south of the summit at roughly 8,100 ft and then begins contouring and descending onward toward Horseshoe Basin and the Boundary Trail. The base of the scramble is exactly where the trail stops climbing. Standing on the plateau at that point, the summit rocks are obvious: they stand up as a small blocky pyramid of about three hundred feet, and there is nothing else nearby that looks like it. Leave the constructed tread and take the cairned, braided path up open talus on the south side of that pyramid; it is easy blocky scrambling and takes only a few minutes. The confirmations at the top are physical and worth checking, because the plateau carries other rises. Benchmark nails are set in the summit rock at the site of the old lookout, and remnants of the lookout's telephone line still run down the northwest slope toward the saddle, so if you can find the wire you are on the right high point. The way to know you have overshot is comfort: if you are walking downhill on good graded tread with the summit rocks behind your shoulder, you have passed the turn and should come back to the trail's high point.

wa_windy_peak_trail.name: Windy Creek trail from Cathedral Driveway
wa_windy_peak_trail.notes: The shortest way up. From the Cathedral Driveway trailhead, a few miles west of Long Swamp on the same road, climb the Windy Creek trail about five miles to its junction with the Windy Peak trail, then go a short distance more to the summit. Some maps wrongly show the trail starting from the Cathedral Driveway trail about half a mile west of the trailhead.
hazards: Trail reported overgrown in stretches from lack of use
Long gravel forest road driving far from any town, no cell coverage
Fully exposed, treeless ridge and summit in wind and lightning
Faint braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch to the true summit
Limited seasonal water on the upper trail
Standing fire-killed timber in wind

wa_windy_peak_trail.name: Boundary Trail from Iron Gate

bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Windy Peak and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. Expect burn. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a free self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

wa_windy_peak_trail.notes: The roughest drive of the three. From FR-39, turn onto FR-3900-500 and follow it about six miles to the Iron Gate trailhead; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended and passenger cars are not advised. Hike north on the Boundary Trail toward Sunny Pass and Horseshoe Basin, then take the Windy Peak trail west to the summit scramble.
hazards: Roughest drive of the three, high clearance advised on the last six miles of road
Fire-killed standing timber comes down in wind; blowdown changes yearly
Water is scarce on the climb and worsens through the season; dependable only at lakes in the basin
Fully exposed alpine tundra and ridge with no shelter when weather arrives from the border
Faint braided cross-country tread over talus for the final stretch to the summit
Remote, no cell coverage
